contentText: Syllabus — Democracy: classical and contemporary theories; different models of democracy — representative, participatory and deliberative. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 6) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning and evolution of democracy; the democracy-development debate (Lee Kuan Yew vs Amartya Sen); classical/normative vs modern/empirical theories (elitist and pluralist — the ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’); Macpherson’s radical/substantive theory; procedural vs substantive democracy; the models — representative, participative and deliberative; and why democracy survived in India. Must-know thinkers:  Herodotus, Plato, Aristotle, J.S. Mill, Schumpeter, Robert Dahl, Macpherson, Pareto, Mosca, Michels, Rousseau, Edmund Burke, Habermas, Joshua Cohen, Nancy Fraser, Hannah Arendt, Carole Pateman, Lee Kuan Yew, Amartya Sen, David Held, Larry Diamond, Huntington. PYQ trend:  deliberative democracy (2019), Macpherson (2018), deliberation vs participation (2017), representative democracy (2016), and the democracy–development / Asian-values debate. Master Questions Q — Critically examine the classical (normative) versus modern (empirical) theories of democracy, and evaluate the elitist-pluralist ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’. Gist — the spine to recall Classical theories ask what democracy OUGHT to be — people’s self-rule and self-development (normative). Modern theories describe how democracy ACTUALLY works — a competition among leaders/elites for votes (empirical). Elitists (Pareto, Michels): the few always rule; Schumpeter: democracy = a ‘competitive struggle for the people’s vote’. Pluralists (Dahl’s ‘polyarchy’): power is dispersed among groups — but Macpherson attacks this ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’ for reducing democracy to a market. Model Answer Macpherson divides democratic theory into  classical (normative)  and  modern (empirical)  families. Classical/normative theories  (rooted in the Greek  polis ) focus on the  substantive  purpose of democracy. The  protective  model ( Locke, Bentham ) values democracy for safeguarding rights and liberties; the  developmental  model ( J.S. Mill, T.H. Green, Laski ) values it for developing human personality. Their weakness — they are ‘divorced from real-world dynamics’. Modern/empirical theories  describe democracy as it actually operates and are  procedural . The  elitist  strand ( Pareto, Mosca, Michels ) holds that a minority always rules: Pareto’s ‘circulation of elites’ and Michels’ ‘iron law of oligarchy’.  Schumpeter  then defines democracy minimally as “an institutional arrangement in which individuals acquire power by a  competitive struggle for the people’s vote ”. The pluralist answer.  Robert Dahl  (in  A Preface to Democratic Theory ) offers  polyarchy  — an ‘approximate democracy’ of decentralised bargaining among relatively autonomous groups (rights, free press, party competition, fair elections). But he later conceded ‘pluralist stagnation’ — organised groups cause ‘government overload’. Macpherson’s critique.  He coins the  ‘Dahl-Schumpeter axis’ : both reduce democracy to procedure and elite competition, so ‘democracy is reduced from humanist aspiration to a market equilibrium system’. Conclusion.  The empirical theories are realistic but hollow; the classical theories are idealistic but impractical — which is why Macpherson seeks to recover democracy’s  substantive, humanist  promise without abandoning its liberal institutions. Q — “Democracy is a humanist aspiration, not a market equilibrium system.” Critically examine Macpherson’s radical/substantive theory of democracy. (UPSC 2018) Gist — the spine to recall Macpherson rejects the elitist idea that democracy is just leaders competing for votes. For him democracy is about empowering people to develop their creative powers, not a market. He distinguishes ‘developmental power’ (using one’s own capacities) from ‘extractive power’ (power over others). True democracy = no one has extractive power and all have equal developmental power — combining social ownership with liberal institutions. Model Answer Macpherson, in  Democratic Theory: Essays in Retrieval , attacks the elitist-pluralist model of  Schumpeter  and  Dahl  (and Bentham’s utilitarian theory) for treating democracy as a mere ‘market equilibrium system’. Against it he argues that ‘democracy is not just a procedure; it is about the  empowerment of the masses ’. The humanist vision.  Democracy’s essence is  creative freedom  — each person ‘realising his creative faculties’. This requires distinguishing two kinds of power:  developmental power  (a person’s ability to use their own capacities creatively) and  extractive power  (power over others, to extract benefits from them). A genuinely democratic society is therefore one ‘where  no one has extractive power over another and all have equal developmental power ’. Achieving it means combining  social ownership  of the means of production with the institutions of liberal democracy, and allocating goods by  need rather than desert . Crucially, Macpherson denies the West a  monopoly on democracy : he accepts three equally valid variants if their conditions are met — liberal democracy ‘with more human touch’, communist systems with full intra-party democracy, and third-world systems ‘legitimised by mass enthusiasm’. Critique.  Norman Barry  objects that Macpherson judges liberal democracy against an ‘ideal version’ rather than against real alternatives — an unfair benchmark. Conclusion.  Macpherson’s radical theory restores the  substantive , emancipatory core that the empirical theories abandoned — reminding us that democracy is finally about human self-development, not just the counting of votes. Q — Distinguish the representative, participative and deliberative models of democracy, and explicate the features and criticisms of representative democracy. (UPSC 2016) Gist — the spine to recall Representative democracy = we elect leaders to rule for us (indirect rule). Participative democracy = citizens themselves take part actively, not just vote once every few years. Deliberative democracy = decisions made through reasoned public discussion, not just counting votes. Representative democracy is practical but criticised for the ‘tyranny of the majority’ and for real power lying with representatives, not people. Model Answer The three models mark a deepening of democracy from voting, to participation, to reasoned discussion. Representative democracy  is indirect rule — citizens elect representatives to govern.  J.S. Mill  (in  Considerations on Representative Government ) called direct democracy the best and representative government ‘the second best’. Its two models of representation are the  delegate  model ( Locke, Bentham  — representatives are bound to the mandate; ‘government is a trust’) and the  trustee/enlightened  model ( Burke  — ‘parliament is the assembly of the nation’, giving representatives judgement). Features  of representative democracy: it is  practicable  in large, complex societies; it relieves citizens of the burden of day-to-day decision-making; and it places government in the hands of those with ‘education and expert knowledge’ — which is why the elitists prefer it. Criticisms.  Mill’s own fear was the  ‘tyranny of the majority’ ;  Rousseau  mocked that ‘the English are free only once in five years’; and  Schumpeter  held it a ‘mistaken belief that sovereignty lies with the people’ — real power rests with representatives.  Gandhi ,  M.N. Roy  and  Jayaprakash Narayan  therefore favoured a ‘party-less democracy’. Conclusion.  Representative democracy is indispensable for scale but insufficient for substance — which is precisely why theorists move on to  participative  democracy (active citizen involvement, Rousseau, Pateman) and  deliberative  democracy (decision by reasoned public argument), each correcting the thinness of mere representation. Q — “Free and fair deliberation is the foundation of democracy.” Examine deliberative democracy and its critics. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Deliberative democracy says legitimacy comes from reasoned public discussion, not merely from counting votes. Habermas: valid decisions need an ‘ideal speech situation’ — everyone can speak freely and only the force of the better argument wins. It gives priority to ‘voice over choice, debate over voting’ (Cohen, Fraser’s ‘counter-public’). Critics: real deliberation is unequal; Waldron defends majority rule, while Dworkin says democracy rests on rights, not just discussion. Model Answer Deliberative democracy holds that the legitimacy of a decision flows not from the mere aggregation of votes but from  reasoned public discussion . As Pericles put it, ‘discussion is an essential prerequisite for any wise action’; democracy is ‘not the game of numbers but the right argument’. Jurgen Habermas  gives it its foundation: legitimacy requires an  ‘ideal speech situation’  and ‘communicative action’ in the  public sphere  (whose model he traces to the ‘coffee houses’ of the West). Its four conditions: an equal right to speak, an equal chance to speak, honest speech, and ‘no force except the force of the better argument’. Joshua Cohen  specifies its features — an ongoing association in which deliberation is the sole route to policy, conducted in a non-coercive setting, accepting pluralism, and treated as the very  source of legitimacy .  Nancy Fraser  adds the feminist idea of a  ‘counter-public’  — an alternative public sphere for subaltern voices. In sum it gives ‘priority to voice over choice, debate over voting’. Critics.  Jeremy Waldron  defends a  majoritarian  model of discussion among political equals;  Ronald Dworkin  replies that ‘the virtues of majoritarianism are exaggerated’ — democracy ‘is based on rights’. In practice, unequal access to the public sphere (weak Panchayati Raj deliberation) limits the ideal. Conclusion.  Deliberation deepens democracy by grounding it in public reason rather than raw numbers — as  Amartya Sen  notes, issues are addressed ‘only when they become matters of public debate’ — but it works only where the conditions of free and equal speech are genuinely met. Q — “Deliberative democracy has no salience without participation, and participatory democracy no credence without deliberation.” Comment. (UPSC 2017) Gist — the spine to recall Participation = people actively taking part; deliberation = people reasoning together before deciding. Participation without deliberation is just numbers/turnout; deliberation without participation is talk by a narrow few. So the two need each other: participation gives deliberation its base, deliberation gives participation its quality. Together (Arendt for participation, Habermas for deliberation) they make democracy substantive, not merely procedural. Model Answer The statement links the two deepening moves beyond representative democracy:  participation  (citizens actively involved, not voting once in five years) and  deliberation  (reasoned discussion before deciding). Each is incomplete without the other. Participation needs deliberation.  Wider participation — of ‘tribals, Dalits, women and minorities’ — confers  legitimacy , and  Hannah Arendt  makes participation in the public sphere the highest human action (man as  zoon politikon ). But participation that is mere presence or head-count ‘has no credence’ unless it involves reasoning together; otherwise it collapses into populism or tokenism (as in weak Panchayati Raj bodies). Deliberation needs participation.  Habermas’  ideal of ‘communicative action’ and  Cohen’s  deliberative features presuppose that the affected actually take part; deliberation confined to a narrow elite ‘has no salience’ because it excludes the very people whose consent legitimises the outcome. Thus the progression is representative → participative → deliberative: representation alone is insufficient, participation supplies the democratic  base , and deliberation supplies its  quality  — ‘deliberation is the heart and soul of democracy’. Conclusion.  Participation and deliberation are two sides of  substantive  democracy: numbers without reason are blind, and reason without numbers is empty. A mature democracy fuses the participative energy of  Arendt  with the deliberative discipline of  Habermas . Q — Examine the democracy–development debate (Lee Kuan Yew vs Amartya Sen). Is democracy a ‘Western value’ incompatible with ‘Asian values’? Gist — the spine to recall Lee Kuan Yew (‘Lee thesis’): democracy slows development; authoritarian, disciplined rule (China model) grows faster. He calls democracy a ‘Western obsession’ clashing with Asian values of discipline and social solidarity. Amartya Sen rebuts: democracy and development are interdependent — ‘development as freedom’, not just growth. Proof: India’s free press prevented famine; democracy has intrinsic, institutional and educational value. Model Answer The debate asks whether democracy helps or hinders development, and whether it suits Asia at all. The Lee thesis.  Lee Kuan Yew  argues democracy obstructs development: he blames Indian democracy for ‘populist policies and extraordinary delay in decision-making’ and praises China’s faster growth, ‘free from the bondages of democratic rule’. Democracy, he says, is a  ‘Western obsession’ ; he prefers a ‘semi-authoritarian guided democracy’ grounded in  Asian values  — communitarianism, discipline and social solidarity. Sen’s rebuttal.  Amartya Sen  holds that democracy and development are ‘not mutually exclusive but interdependent’, and that ‘development cannot be equated merely to economic growth’ — it is  ‘development as freedom’ . The Lee thesis rests on ‘questionable assumptions and insufficient evidence’: democratic  Botswana  grew fast, while authoritarian China suffered famine. The famine argument.  Sen’s decisive point: ‘India has suffered no famine since independence’, whereas some 30 million died in China’s 1958–61 famine — because a democracy’s  free press  forces ‘corrective action’. He praises the  Kerala model  over the Gujarat model. Three values of democracy  (Sen):  intrinsic  (a source of self-worth),  institutional  (it makes government accountable) and  educational  (it makes citizens aware and responsible). Conclusion.  Democracy is not a merely Western import: as  Sen’s   The Argumentative Indian  shows, deliberation and tolerance have deep Indian roots. Development is best secured  through  democracy, not by suspending it — the Lee thesis mistakes a short-run trade-off for a permanent one. Q — “Good governance is achievable only by strengthening grass-root democracy.” Discuss participatory democracy, the global democratic deficit, and why democracy survived in India. Gist — the spine to recall Grass-root (participatory) democracy brings power close to people — the basis of good governance and inclusive development. Rousseau is its pioneer: ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’; participation is a precondition for freedom. Globally there is a ‘democratic deficit’ — Held’s ‘cosmopolitan democracy’ seeks to fix it. India’s democracy survived due to the freedom movement, elite commitment (Nehru), British institutions and its argumentative tradition. Model Answer Good governance — accountable, participatory, inclusive rule — depends on deepening democracy at the base.  Participatory democracy  brings decision-making close to citizens;  Rousseau , its pioneer, held that ‘sovereignty cannot be represented’ and that participation is ‘a precondition for freedom’. Forms and benefits.  It takes  institutionalised  forms (Panchayati Raj, RTI, citizen charters, the right to recall) and  non-institutionalised  forms (social movements).  Carole Pateman  identifies three benefits — it is ‘educative’ for citizens, realises the general will, and makes democracy inclusive — while  Elinor Ostrom  shows communities can sustainably manage common resources. The global democratic deficit.  Democracy has spread among states, but the  world order  has not become more democratic —  Stiglitz  notes the ‘democratic deficit’ of global institutions.  David Held’s   cosmopolitan model of democracy  proposes reforming the UN Security Council, IMF and World Bank, regional parliaments, and even global referenda to close the gap. Why democracy survived in India  (against the third-world trend): the elite’s commitment (Nehru’s faith in democracy), the legacy of the national movement and of British parliamentary institutions, India’s  argumentative tradition  (Sen), enabling constitutional provisions (a free press, independent judiciary and Election Commission), its very size and diversity, and the strict separation of civil and military authority. Conclusion.  Good governance is ultimately ‘bottom-up’: strengthening grass-root democracy makes government responsive and legitimate, while reforming global institutions extends the same democratic logic beyond the nation-state — exactly the direction India’s resilient democracy points toward.
